HEADLINE: Ban it or restrict it?;
Designated-area approach proves more costly
BYLINE: By JAMES BRAHAM
BODY:
Corporate smoking policies have become, pardon the expression, a burning
issue.
The questions no longer concern whether to institute a policy. Rather, they
ask how restrictive the policy should be: Designated smoking areas? What about
private offices, often a particularly touchy subject? Or a complete
company-wide ban? And what steps are involved?
Some of the largest companies have found that a total ban is the answer.
It's the easiest and most effective way to achieve a smoke-free environment.
Pacific Northwest Bell (PNB), for example, prohibits smoking in any of its
750 buildings. It adopted this policy two years ago when its previous "mixed
bag of smoking and non-smoking" didn't work. Begun in 1983, the earlier policy
outlawed smoking in meeting rooms and in about two-thirds of cafeteria space; it
also let individual work groups designate their areas smoking or not.
Result: "hassles" and complaints about drifting smoke, along with union
insistence that all employees and locations be treated identically. For these
reasons, plus the realization that the only way to eliminate drifting smoke
would be to ventilate it outside (prohibitively expensive), the Seattle-based
company adopted a complete smoking ban.
BRIEF POLICY. It's stated simply: "To protect the health and safety of PNB
employees, there will be no smoking in any company facility." This memo was sent
to all 15,O00 employees from President Andrew Smith, who noted that the company
is not recruiting employees to quit, that smoking is a matter of personal
choice.
The complete ban has provoked little negative reaction. "When we made the
policy clear, straightforward, and communicated the rationale behind it, it
became a moot point," says Leonard Beil, director of human-resources planning.
A number of companies will begin (or extend) smoking restrictions at the
start of 1988.
Federal Express Corp., with nearly 50,O00 employees, will take the final step
in its two-year, phase-in approach toward a no-smoking work environment.
